rrel-01-c2.text: Fourth Lateran Council (1215). Fourth Lateran Council: Canons, Canon 62. Fordham University Medieval Sourcebook.
rrel-01-c2.quote: In the future old relics may not be exhibited outside of a vessel or exposed for sale.
rrel-01-c2.claim: The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) banned the sale of relics and their display outside a reliquary

rrel-01-c2.text: Holy See (1983). Code of Canon Law, Book IV, Title IV, canon 1190. Vatican (vatican.va).
rrel-01-c2.quote: It is absolutely forbidden to sell sacred relics.
rrel-01-c2.claim: the current Code of Canon Law (1983) states that selling sacred relics is "absolutely forbidden."

rrel-01-c3.text: Second Council of Nicaea (787). Canons of the Seventh Ecumenical Council, Canon VII, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, Vol. 14. New Advent (Schaff and Wace, eds.).
rrel-01-c3.quote: if any bishop from this time forward is found consecrating a temple without holy relics
rrel-01-c3.claim: The Second Council of Nicaea (787), called mainly to restore the veneration of icons after Byzantine iconoclasm, ruled in its seventh canon that churches consecrated without relics must have them deposited

rrel-01-c3.text: Sister Vajira and Francis Story (trans.) (1998). Maha-parinibbana Sutta: Last Days of the Buddha (DN 16). Access to Insight (Buddhist Publication Society).
rrel-01-c3.quote: So it came about that there were eight stupas for the relics, a ninth for the urn, and a tenth for the ashes.
rrel-01-c3.claim: A Brahmin named Dona divided the bones into eight shares. He kept the measuring vessel, and a latecomer clan received the embers, making ten monuments in all.

rrel-03-c2.quote: We learn from St. Cyril of Jerusalem (before 350) that the wood of the Cross, discovered c. 318, was already distributed throughout the world
rrel-03-c2.claim: Wood venerated as the cross was in Jerusalem by about 350, though, when Bishop Cyril remarked that fragments of it had already filled the world.

rrel-02-c3.text: M. Ott (1911). St. Nicholas of Myra. The Catholic Encyclopedia.
rrel-02-c3.quote: In 1087 Italian merchants stole his body at Myra, bringing it to Bari in Italy.
rrel-02-c3.claim: In spring 1087 sailors and merchants from Bari, in southern Italy, sailed to Myra

rrel-04-c2.text: (1873). The Sacred Tooth of Buddha. The Sacred Tooth of Buddha (1873).
rrel-04-c2.quote: the tooth was placed in a mortar by the archbishop in presence of the court, and reduced to powder and burned, its ashes being scattered over the sea.
rrel-04-c2.claim: In 1561 the tooth was publicly ground in a mortar and burned, and its ashes were thrown into the water.

rrel-04-c1.text: (1873). The Sacred Tooth of Buddha. The Sacred Tooth of Buddha (1873).
rrel-04-c1.quote: left canine tooth was carried to Dantapura, the capital of Kalinga, where it was preserved for eight hundred years.
rrel-04-c1.claim: gave it to the king of Kalinga, on India's east coast, who enshrined it at Dantapura

rrel-05-c2.quote: The body is practically mummified, covered with patches of mildew and quite a notable layer of salts
rrel-05-c2.claim: In 1919 a doctor described it as practically mummified, with patches of mold and a layer of salts.

rrel-05-c2.quote: an imprint of her face was molded, which was used to create a wax mask to be placed on her body.
rrel-05-c2.claim: A thin wax mask was therefore molded, using photographs and an imprint of her face

rrel-06-c2.text: P. E. Damon et al (1989). Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin. Nature.
rrel-06-c2.quote: The results of radiocarbon measurements at Arizona, Oxford and Zurich yield a calibrated calendar age range.
rrel-06-c2.claim: sent to three laboratories, at the University of Arizona, the University of Oxford and ETH Zurich

rrel-06-c2.text: P. E. Damon et al (1989). Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin. Nature.
rrel-06-c2.quote: The age of the shroud is obtained as AD 1260-1390, with at least 95% confidence.
rrel-06-c2.claim: the linen dated to 1260 to 1390 CE at 95% confidence
